title: Activepieces vs Temporal for Workflow Automation
summary: Activepieces vs Temporal solve different problems: use Activepieces for broken business processes between apps, Temporal when application code must resume.
body_markdown:
## Pricing, hosting and admin controls compared


Activepieces' cloud plans start at $20 a month, while a self-hosted Temporal cluster costs **$480 to $790 a month** in infrastructure alone, so the two bills measure different things.


### Pricing models and entry prices


You pay a fixed amount and the vendor runs the servers:[Plus at $20 a month and Team at $200 a month](https://www.activepieces.com/pricing) . Temporal's server is software you run yourself, so the figure is a hosting bill.


Both sit side by side in the chart, with the Temporal bar as a range of $480 to $790 a month, so your monthly bill will depend on actual usage.


When a worker stops polling, someone has to be on call, and that salary will usually outweigh the infrastructure line.


### Self-hosting and licences


There's no licence fee, because Temporal's server is open source under the MIT licence. The price is operational: a database, the server services, and worker processes you deploy alongside your own application code.


Self-hosting a workflow builder is a lighter install, but enterprise self-hosting goes through a sales conversation rather than a price list.


On Temporal Cloud, SAML-based single sign-on is supported. On a self-hosted server, authentication and authorisation are plugin points you wire to your own identity provider, which means writing and maintaining that integration.


For a builder-style tool, SSO beyond the Team tier is quoted by sales.


Comparing $20 with $480 conflates software licensing with operational costs: one is a subscription, the other a floor for running infrastructure, meaning the apparent price difference is deceptive without your actual infrastructure expenses.


Two mistakes recur. One is leaving out staffing, since an unattended cluster fails at 2am like any other service. The other is budgeting for one environment, when staging and production roughly double the infrastructure line.


If your team is non-engineers automating app-to-app processes, the cluster will rarely be justified. If your team already runs its own services, with failure-critical code, you are already paying for that operational overhead.
